metaDescription: Six automatic motion-sensor trash cans compared by capacity, stay-open options, filters and finishes, from a 13-gallon plastic bin to a 24-gallon steel giant.
introParagraphs: An automatic trash can swaps a pedal or a push-flap for a motion sensor, so the lid lifts when your hand or a plate passes over it. The idea is simple and the payoff is real if you cook often, carry things with both hands or simply dislike touching a lid. The catch is that sensors differ in reliability, in how long they stay open and in what they need for power.

This lineup spans a wide range. The BestOffice plastic and the two Ninestars bins hold 13 gallons, the EKO matte stainless holds 13 gallons with a soft-close lid, and the EKO Mirage X steps up to 80 liters. The iTouchless sits at the top with a 24-gallon, 91-liter body and a carbon filter in the box.

We evaluated the six on listing specs and buyer feedback themes, comparing capacity, stay-open features, odor management and finish. The goal is to help you pick a sensor bin that fits your kitchen size and your habits, not just the one with the flashiest lid.

products.name: EKO 13.2 Gallon Touchless Motion Sensor Kitchen Trash Can
products.description:
This EKO is the balanced choice among the automatic bins. At 50 liters it handles a standard kitchen bag, and the matte stainless steel finish is described as anti-fingerprint, so the front stays presentable after a day of cooking. The listing frames the lid action as smooth and seamless, which is the point of paying more for a sensor can in the first place.

The soft-close lid is the detail that separates a good automatic can from a noisy one. Instead of dropping shut, the lid settles down quietly, so a late-night trip to the kitchen does not wake anyone. Hands stay off the lid completely, which helps with raw meat, sticky dough and greasy plates.

Compared with the iTouchless 24-gallon, it is far smaller and easier to place in a normal kitchen. Compared with the EKO Mirage X at 80 liters, it gives up volume for a lighter footprint. And against the BestOffice plastic, you pay for a steel body with better finish control. For most kitchens it is the sensible automatic option.

products.name: EKO Mirage X 80 Liter Motion Sensor Trash Can
products.description:
The Mirage X is built for kitchens that produce a lot of waste. Its 80-liter body, which the listing equates to 21.1 gallons, holds noticeably more than the 13-gallon bins, and the listing adds that it can serve as a recycling bin as well. The stainless steel carries an anti-fingerprint finish for a clean exterior.

Its stand-out feature is a press-to-open option that keeps the lid open for 20 minutes. When you are clearing a large pile of scraps after a dinner party, or cutting vegetables directly into the bin, that hold-open mode saves you from waving at the sensor again and again. It is a practical answer to the main complaint about sensor lids, which is that they close right as you reach for them.

The tradeoff is size. It takes more floor space than the EKO 13.2 gallon and demands larger bags, so measure carefully. Against the iTouchless, which is bigger still, the Mirage X is the more compact way to get a high-capacity sensor bin. If you entertain or cook for many, it is the standout.
products.bestFor: Large households that want high capacity and a stay-open mode.
pros: Eighty liters holds far more waste

products.name: iTouchless 24 Gallon Motion Sensor Trash Can with Odor Filter
products.description:
The iTouchless is the largest can on this list, at 24 gallons or 91 liters. It suits families that fill a bag in a day, busy kitchens and anyone who would rather take the trash out less often. The listing highlights a tall frame that lets you scrape plates while standing upright, which can spare your back from repeated bending.

It uses what the maker calls Sensor 2.0 technology, described as opening instantly without false triggers. A continuous carbon filter, branded AbsorbX, is included to trap and neutralize garbage smells, which is a feature the 13-gallon sensor bins here do not list. The body is stainless steel.

The size is also the drawback. A 24-gallon can dominates a small kitchen and needs large liners, and a bin that big invites you to leave waste sitting longer. The filter also needs replacing over time. Compared with the EKO Mirage X at 80 liters, it offers more volume and an included filter, but takes more room. If your kitchen has space and your household is big, it is the volume leader.
products.bestFor: Big households with space for a very large sensor bin.

products.name: Ninestars 13 Gallon Rectangular Automatic Trash Can
products.description:
The Ninestars rectangular model puts its effort into fitting a real kitchen. A 13-gallon body with a rectangular profile sits flat against a wall or cabinet, and the listing says the capacity is enough for bulky takeout boxes. A quick wave opens the lid, so there is nothing to press with a foot or a hand.

The lid is described as precision-fit, closing softly and securely to seal in stubborn odors. That combination of sealing and gentle closing suits a bin that sits near a dining table, where noise and smell are both noticeable. The motion sensor spares your hands during messy prep work.

What it lacks is the stay-open option that the oval Ninestars offers, and the larger size of the EKO Mirage X. It is also a plain functional design rather than a statement piece. Compared with the BestOffice plastic, it adds a rectangular shape that wastes less corner space. If you want a tidy, wall-hugging sensor bin that does the job without fuss, this is a dependable pick.
products.bestFor: Kitchens where a rectangular bin fits flush against a wall.
pros: Rectangular shape sits flush to walls
Lid closes softly and seals in odors
Wave opening keeps hands clean
Handles bulky takeout packaging

products.name: Ninestars 13 Gallon Oval Automatic Trash Can
products.description:
The oval Ninestars adds something its rectangular sibling does not: a button that keeps the lid resting open. When you are loading several items, such as cleaning out a fridge or tipping scraps from a large board, you tap the button and the lid stays up until you are done. For the rest of the time, a wave of the hand opens it as normal.

The wide oval opening is meant to handle bulky waste and gives you more room to aim. The smooth profile is described as space-friendly, and the 13-gallon capacity is the standard kitchen size. A precision-fit lid closes softly to help seal in odors.

Oval shapes waste a bit more wall space than rectangles because the curves leave gaps. Compared with the rectangular Ninestars, you gain the hold-open convenience but lose a little footprint efficiency. Compared with the EKO Mirage X, which holds the lid open for 20 minutes, the Ninestars does it by button but at 13 gallons rather than 80 liters. It is a smart pick for cooks who like to clear the counter in one go.
products.bestFor: Cooks who clear lots of scraps at once and want the lid held open.

products.name: BestOffice 13 Gallon Plastic Touchless Trash Can
products.description:
This BestOffice uses plastic where the other sensor bins here use steel. The body is made from PP plastic that the listing calls waterproof and anti-scratch, with a sleek oval shape. The 13-gallon, 50-liter size fits standard kitchen bags, and the touchless sensors open and close the lid quietly.

Plastic gives the bin a lighter feel, which helps when you carry it to the curb, and it is not prone to denting. It also does not show fingerprints the way steel can. The listing positions it as modern and stylish, suited to a kitchen or other rooms.

What you give up is the premium look and the weight that makes steel bins feel stable. The listing does not mention a stay-open button, a filter or a soft-close damper, so it is a simpler tool than the EKO and Ninestars models. For a household that wants hands-free convenience in a light, scratch-resistant body, it is a straightforward choice, though the EKO 13.2 gallon is more refined.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A sensor can is only convenient if it opens when you want it and stays closed when you do not. The iTouchless markets Sensor 2.0 as avoiding false triggers, while other listings simply promise smooth operation. Pay attention to how far from the lid the sensor reacts. A bin that opens when you walk by is annoying, and one that needs a close wave is frustrating.

The usual complaint about sensor lids is that they close while you are still loading. The EKO Mirage X keeps its lid open for 20 minutes with a press-to-open feature, and the oval Ninestars has a button that holds the lid open. Rectangular models without that option need a hand wave at every addition. If you often dump a whole cutting board of scraps, prioritize a hold-open mode.

The 13-gallon bins, including the EKO 13.2 gallon and both Ninestars, suit standard kitchens, the EKO Mirage X offers 80 liters, and the iTouchless reaches 24 gallons. More capacity cuts trips outside but takes floor space and demands larger liners. Measure your gap and your overhead clearance first. A huge can in a small kitchen becomes an obstacle.

Sensor bins need electricity, usually from batteries, and listings do not always spell it out. Plan to buy and swap cells, and keep spares when you can. A bin whose sensor dies in the middle of dinner is no more hygienic than a pedal can. Check the manual for the exact battery type and expected life before relying on it.

Automatic lids that close fully help contain smells. The Ninestars models describe an odor-sealing lid, the iTouchless includes an AbsorbX carbon filter, and the EKO bins focus on a soft-close lid. A filter wears out and needs replacing, and no lid cures a bag left too long. Empty the bin often when you cook strong ingredients.

Stainless steel, as on the EKO and iTouchless bins, looks premium and can be fingerprint resistant, while PP plastic on the BestOffice is light and scratch resistant. Steel feels stable but can dent, and plastic resists dents but can look less refined. Choose the material that matches your kitchen and how much cleaning you want to do. A sensor window that gets splashed with grease will misread, so a finish that wipes clean in one pass, like the matte steel on the EKO 13.2 gallon, saves repeat trouble.

faq.q: Are automatic trash cans worth the extra cost?
faq.a: They are if you value hands-free use, particularly when cooking or carrying items. A sensor bin removes the need to touch a lid or press a pedal, which also keeps the lid itself cleaner over the years. The tradeoff is the need for power and the chance of occasional sensor quirks.

faq.q: What powers an automatic trash can?
faq.a: Many use batteries, though some can use other power sources. The BestOffice steel model from the same maker uses four C batteries, so check the manual for your exact bin. Keep spare cells on hand.

faq.q: Why does my lid keep closing on me?
faq.a: Standard sensor lids close after a short delay. Choose a bin with a hold-open feature, such as the EKO Mirage X for 20 minutes or the oval Ninestars with its button. That way you can empty a whole board without waving again. Models without that feature, such as the rectangular Ninestars, are better for people who drop in a few items at a time.

faq.q: How do I reduce odors in a sensor bin?
faq.a: Use a bin with a sealing lid, like the Ninestars, or a carbon filter, like the iTouchless. Empty the bag often and wipe the rim. Filters need replacing over time.

Thirteen gallons fits most kitchens, the EKO Mirage X offers 80 liters for big households, and the iTouchless holds 24 gallons. Measure your space first. A very large can may crowd a small kitchen, and it also needs bigger liners that you must keep in stock. If you are unsure, start with the EKO 13.2 gallon, which fits standard bags and most kitchen gaps.

faq.q: Can a sensor trash can get dirty inside?
faq.a: Yes, as any bin can. Wipe the lid and the sensor window with a soft cloth and rinse the inside when a bag leaks. Do not submerge electronics. If the lid ever acts strangely after a cleaning, let everything dry fully and check the batteries before assuming the sensor has failed.

faq.q: Is plastic or steel better for a sensor bin?
faq.a: Steel looks premium and can resist fingerprints, as on the EKO and iTouchless bins. Plastic, as on the BestOffice, is lighter and scratch resistant. The choice comes down to style, weight and your cleaning preferences.
